analysis.one_liner: Replaces the progressive income tax with a flat 15% tax and repeals the estate tax and most tax credits.
analysis.headline: A single House member introduced the flat-tax bill with zero cosponsors; it never got a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the entire income tax structure with a flat 15% tax on wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits above a standard deduction ($25,000 for a married couple). It would repeal the alternative minimum tax, all of the tax credits in Part IV of the tax code — which includes the child tax credit and the Earned Income Tax Credit — and the estate and gift taxes entirely. Because taxable income is defined only as wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment compensation, income from investments — capital gains, dividends, and interest — would not be taxed at all. It would also cut the corporate rate from 21% to 15% and levy a 15% tax on noncash benefits (like health coverage) provided by tax-exempt organizations and governments to their employees.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and wealthy households gain the most: investment income like capital gains, dividends, and interest is left out of the taxable income definition entirely, the estate and gift taxes disappear, and no tax above 15% would ever apply. Business owners gain from a 15% business rate, down from the current 21% corporate rate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large-estate heirs

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps the individual tax rate at a flat 15% on wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation above the standard deduction, so no earner would ever pay a higher bracket rate.
The new taxable income definition includes only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, leaving capital gains, dividends, and interest income outside the tax.
The bill repeals the estate and gift taxes entirely for deaths and gifts after 2022, eliminating the tax on very large inheritances.
The bill sets a flat 15% tax on business taxable income for every person engaged in business, replacing the current 21% corporate rate with a lower one.
The bill repeals the alternative minimum tax, which currently limits how much high earners can reduce their taxes through deductions.

analysis.who_pays: Working families lose the child tax credit and the Earned Income Tax Credit, which the bill repeals, while paying 15% on wages above the deduction; the Treasury loses revenue from the estate tax repeal and the untaxed investment income, with nothing in the bill to replace it. Employees of tax-exempt organizations and governments would see their noncash benefits, like employer health coverage, hit with a 15% employer tax.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Part IV of the tax code wipes out the child tax credit and the Earned Income Tax Credit, raising taxes on many low- and moderate-income working families even after the larger standard deduction.

Because taxable income covers only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, capital gains, dividends, and interest would go completely untaxed — a wage earner and a person living off investments with the same income would be taxed very differently.
The bill repeals the estate and gift taxes and much of the existing income tax with no replacement revenue anywhere in the bill.
Unemployment compensation, which many households rely on after a job loss, remains taxable at the full 15% rate.

The bill imposes a 15% tax on noncash compensation such as employer health coverage provided by tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local governments, raising the cost of those benefits for their employees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow overwhelmingly to the top: untaxed investment income, no estate tax, no AMT, and a 15% business rate. The costs fall on working families, who would lose the two largest refundable credits supporting low- and moderate-income households and see public revenue shrink with nothing replacing it. It is a large tax cut for concentrated wealth paid for by wage earners and the Treasury, and its single-sponsor, no-cosponsor status reflects that few members of either party were willing to back it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up; with no cosponsors and the Congress ending days later, it simply expired.

narrative.text: Louie Gohmert introduced the bill on December 22, 2022 — the last stretch of the 117th Congress — and no other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which is the full extent of its action history; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and an unpassed bill dies when a Congress ends, so the flat tax never came close to a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working families who rely on the child tax credit and the Earned Income Tax Credit are better off the bill never advanced, as are taxpayers who would have paid 15% on unemployment benefits; the estate-tax repeal and untaxed investment income its backers wanted did not happen.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working families who claim tax credits

for.name: Louie Gohmert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 22, 2022, the final days of the Congress.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill after its referral; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the estate and gift taxes outright and leave capital gains, dividends, and interest out of taxable income entirely. Their gain would come at the cost of revenue that funds services and of a tax code that no longer taxes investment income.
The bill would replace the 21% corporate rate with a 15% tax on business income and repeal the alternative minimum tax. The revenue gap would fall on other taxpayers.
A new 15% tax would apply to noncash benefits these employers provide, such as health coverage, effectively making benefits costlier for their employees.
Repealing Part IV of the tax code eliminates the child tax credit and the Earned Income Tax Credit, the main tax supports for low- and moderate-income workers.
